summary: Psalm 84 opens with longing for Yahweh's dwellings and courts, picturing even small birds finding a place near the altars. It then follows pilgrims whose strength is in God as they pass through hardship toward Zion, and it closes with prayer for God's anointed and trust in Yahweh as sun, shield, giver, and protector.
whyItMatters: Within Book III of Psalms, this chapter gives a bright sanctuary song inside a darker section of the collection. It centers desire for God's house, the journey toward worship, and trust in Yahweh without explaining the exact historical situation behind the prayer.

context.author: The heading associates the psalm with the sons of Korah and gives a musical direction; the exact origin and force of such headings are debated.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving Psalms as public and private prayer.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; assigning one date to this psalm from this chapter alone would overstate what is known.
context.setting: The poem is oriented toward Yahweh's house, altars, courts, pilgrimage, and Zion, within the worship world of the Psalter.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, using longing, blessing, pilgrimage imagery, direct petition, and compact images such as sun and shield.

outline.heading: Longing for Yahweh's dwellings
outline.note: The psalm begins with a heading, then praises Yahweh's dwellings and courts, imagines birds near the altars, and calls those who dwell in God's house blessed.

outline.heading: Pilgrims strengthened on the way
outline.note: Those whose strength is in God move through the valley of Weeping, find springs and blessing, and appear before God in Zion.

outline.heading: Prayer for God to hear and look
outline.note: The speaker asks Yahweh, God of Armies, to hear, and asks God to look on the face of his anointed.

outline.heading: One day in the courts
outline.note: The speaker values a single day in God's courts above a thousand elsewhere and prefers lowly nearness to God's house over life in wickedness.

outline.heading: Trust in Yahweh of Armies
outline.note: The psalm ends by describing Yahweh as sun and shield, giver of grace and glory, and blessing the one who trusts in him.

keyVerses.text: My soul longs, and even faints for the courts of Yahweh. My heart and my flesh cry out for the living God.
keyVerses.why: This verse names the intensity of the psalm's desire: the whole person longs for Yahweh's courts and for the living God.

keyVerses.text: Blessed are those whose strength is in you, who have set their hearts on a pilgrimage.
keyVerses.why: This verse shifts from those dwelling in God's house to those traveling toward it, making pilgrimage a central movement of the chapter.

keyVerses.text: For a day in your courts is better than a thousand. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the psalm's strongest comparison: nearness to God's courts is valued above length of days or more comfortable association with wickedness.

keyVerses.text: For Yahweh God is a sun and a shield. Yahweh will give grace and glory. He withholds no good thing from those who walk blamelessly.
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers the psalm's trust into two images and a claim about Yahweh's generosity toward those who walk blamelessly.

themes: Trust in Yahweh as sun and shield

questions.question: Who are the sons of Korah in the heading?
questions.answer: The chapter's heading says this is “A Psalm by the sons of Korah.” Psalms is an anthology with headings that may name performers, collections, genres, instruments, dedications, or associations. Readers differ on how much a heading proves about authorship, so it is best to treat the line as part of the received psalm without turning it into more certainty than it gives.

questions.question: What does “On an instrument of Gath” mean?
questions.answer: The heading preserves a musical direction: “On an instrument of Gath.” Musical directions are preserved in Psalms, but ancient melodies and the exact force of several performance terms are lost. This tells readers the psalm belonged to a performed or sung tradition, but not exactly what the sound was.

questions.question: Why does the speaker mention a sparrow and a swallow near the altars?
questions.answer: The birds are pictured as having a home and a nest near Yahweh's altars. The image intensifies the speaker's longing: even small creatures seem to have the nearness to God's dwelling that the speaker desires. The verse does not explain whether the birds are literal, poetic, or both; the point in the poem is their settled place near the altars.

questions.question: What does “Selah” mean here?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears after the blessing on those who dwell in God's house and again after the prayer for God to listen. Translations often preserve this Hebrew sound because its exact instruction is no longer known. It likely signals something about performance or pause, but its exact function remains uncertain.

questions.question: What is the “valley of Weeping”?
questions.answer: The psalm says pilgrims pass through “the valley of Weeping” and make it “a place of springs.” The line presents a hard or sorrowful place being transformed along the way to appearing before God in Zion. Interpreters debate whether the valley names a specific place or functions mainly as a poetic image; the chapter itself does not settle that question.

questions.question: Who is “your anointed” in verse 9?
questions.answer: The psalm asks God to “look at the face of your anointed.” In Psalms, the anointed one can be connected with the king, and later Jewish and Christian readers also connect royal language with messianic hope. In this chapter, the immediate text gives a prayer for the anointed but does not identify the person by name.

questions.question: Is the psalm saying temple worship is better than every other kind of life?
questions.answer: Verse 10 uses a strong comparison: one day in God's courts is better than a thousand, and being a doorkeeper in God's house is preferred to dwelling in the tents of wickedness. The point is the speaker's valuation of nearness to God, not a full social program or a denial that faithful life can happen outside the courts. The psalm speaks poetically and devotionally from the world of worship and pilgrimage.

questions.question: What does it mean that Yahweh is “a sun and a shield”?
questions.answer: The verse uses two images for Yahweh: “a sun and a shield.” In the immediate line, those images sit beside giving grace and glory and withholding no good thing from those who walk blamelessly. The psalm does not unpack the images mechanically, but together they present Yahweh as source of life, favor, and protection.

questions.question: Does “He withholds no good thing” mean nothing painful will happen to trusting people?
questions.answer: The verse says Yahweh “withholds no good thing from those who walk blamelessly,” but the same psalm has already imagined pilgrims passing through the valley of Weeping. The Psalter as a whole includes both confident trust and suffering prayer, so this line should not be isolated as a guarantee that faithful people avoid hardship. In this chapter, trust includes movement through sorrow toward God, not denial that sorrow exists.

glossary.def: Places where Yahweh is said to dwell; in this psalm the word opens the speaker's praise of Yahweh's worship space.
The areas of Yahweh's house that the speaker longs for and values more than a thousand days elsewhere.
A preserved performance marker in Psalms whose exact meaning is uncertain.
A journey toward worship; in this psalm it describes people whose hearts are set on appearing before God in Zion.
A person marked out in relation to God; in this psalm the speaker asks God to look at this person's face.
